title: Debugging production
subtitle: When production breaks, first stop the harm, then find the cause with data, one hypothesis at a time.

c.v: On 18 November 2025 at 11:05 UTC, Cloudflare changed the access rights on one of its databases. From 11:20, its network began to fail to deliver core traffic. Many websites behind Cloudflare showed error pages.
An automated test caught the problem at 11:31. At 11:35 the team opened an incident call.
The team first thought it was a huge DDoS attack. Two things pointed that way. Cloudflare had recently fought a wave of very large attacks. And its
, which runs outside Cloudflare, went down at the same time. That was a coincidence, but it made some people think an attacker was hitting both.

The errors were strange, too. The network failed, recovered, then failed again. The real cause was a file of bot features that was rebuilt every five minutes. The database cluster was being updated step by step, so each run could make a good file or a bad one.

The bad file came from the database change. A query started to return duplicate rows, so the file doubled in size. The proxy had a limit of 200 features and normally used about 60. The bigger file went over the limit, and the proxy failed.
At 14:24 the team stopped making new files, and a test with an older file worked. By 14:30 core traffic was mostly flowing again. Every service was back at 17:06.
Note what misled them: a coincidence, and a symptom that came and went.
In production, real users are hurting while you debug. So you have two goals, in this order:
Then fix it so it does not come back.
Google's SRE book says that in a big outage, you may want to start hunting for the
at once. Its advice: "Ignore that instinct!" Instead, make the system work as well as it can for now.
After that, use a loop. Look at the data. Make one guess, called a
. Test it. If the test says no, make the next guess. The book calls this the hypothetico-deductive method.
Mitigate first, debug second. Then let data, not the loudest opinion, choose between hypotheses, and test them one at a time.

The fastest safe action is usually one of these:
the last deploy or config change. In one Google emergency, an engineer pushed another config change to roll back the first one, and services began to recover.
The SRE book gives examples: send traffic away from a broken cluster, or turn off subsystems to reduce load.
Fast action can still save evidence, such as logs.
Take a minute to save logs, a heap dump, or one bad host out of traffic. If you feel overwhelmed, pull in more people.
A system tends to keep running until something acts on it, such as a config change or a new kind of load. So start with recent changes.
settings, feature flags, firewall rules, generated data files.

In the Cloudflare story, the change was in a database, not in the proxy that failed.
So look beyond your own service.

Saturation means extra work the resource cannot handle yet, often waiting in a queue.
Tom Wilkie, who created RED, says RED cares about how happy your users are, and USE about how happy your machines are.
Start with RED to find the service that hurts, then use USE on its machines.
4. Test one hypothesis at a time
Write each hypothesis down, for example: "The new
is too small." Say what data would prove it wrong.
Test the most likely idea first, and think about risk to the system: "when you hear hoofbeats, think of horses not zebras."
Take notes on each idea, each test and each result. Do not ignore a clear "no": negative results are useful too.
Split the problem in two, again and again. The SRE book calls this divide and conquer, or
what happened in the minute before the first error?
is one region bad and the others fine?
do errors come only from hosts on the new build?
is it one customer, one card type, one app version?
Each good split roughly halves the search.

Sometimes you must test in production. Change one thing, on one host or a

The SRE book lists traps that send teams the wrong way.

The worst trap is many people changing things at once. Google tells of an engineer whose change, made without telling anyone, made an outage worse. Its rule: only the operations team changes the system during an incident.

PagerDuty adds: "the Incident Commander is NOT a resolver."

As Google puts it, you cannot fix people, but you can fix systems and processes.
Blame makes engineers stay silent, and silence makes incidents longer.

sections.name: At work
sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: Ask in the first five minutes: "Are users hurting? What changed in the last hour? How fast can we undo it?"
Make rollback and flag-off a single, tested command. Practise it on a quiet day.
Keep one timeline in the incident channel: each change, hypothesis and test, with the time.
Say hypotheses as "I think X, because Y. If I am right, we will see Z." When a theory fits too well, look for data that would break it.
Write the postmortem within a few days. Name systems and gaps, not people. Give every
"Here are 2,000 log lines from the checkout service between 14:00 and 14:20. Group the errors by type. For each group, give the count, the first time it appeared and three example trace IDs."
"Here is our deploy log and config history for the last 24 hours. List every change that happened in the 30 minutes before 14:05."
"Draft a blameless postmortem from this incident channel export. Use 'the on-call engineer', not names. Mark every claim you could not find in the export."
Every cause the AI gives is only a hypothesis.
It can sound sure and still be wrong. Ask for the exact log lines, then open them yourself.
The counts and times match your dashboards. Summaries can drop or merge errors.
The AI saw the whole time window, not just the part that fit in its context.
No secrets or personal data went into the prompt.

You still do the reasoning. In Anthropic's January 2026 trial, 52 mostly junior engineers learned a new Python library, Trio. One group had an AI assistant. The AI group scored 50% on the quiz and the hand-coding group 67%. The biggest gap was on debugging questions.
People who asked for explanations and conceptual answers learned more.
The study was small and tested learning only shortly after the task.

q.v: Checkout errors jump from 0.2% to 6% ten minutes after a deploy. What do you do first?

options.v: Read the new code until you find the bug.
Roll back the deploy, then investigate with the logs you saved.
Wait 30 minutes to see if the errors go away.

why.v: Stop the harm first. A rollback is fast and usually safe, and you can find the bug after users are fine.

q.v: Errors come only from servers running version 4.2. Servers on 4.1 are fine. What have you just done?

why.v: Splitting the traffic into two groups narrows the search. It does not yet prove the cause, but it tells you where to look.

q.v: Which method gives you rate, errors and duration for each service?

why.v: RED is for services and their requests. USE checks utilization, saturation and errors for resources like CPU and disks.

q.v: During an incident, three engineers each try a different fix at the same time. Why is this a problem?

options.v: It is not a problem. More fixes means a faster recovery.
You cannot tell which change helped or hurt, and changes can make the outage worse.

why.v: Google's SRE book says only the operations team should change the system during an incident, so every change is known and coordinated.

q.v: An AI assistant reads your logs and says, "The root cause is a memory leak in the cache." What should you do?

options.v: Accept it. The AI read more logs than you can.
Ask which log lines prove it, then check them and test the idea yourself.
Restart the cache to fix it.

why.v: AI can summarise logs well but can also give a cause that sounds right and is wrong. Treat it as one hypothesis to test.
